claims.text: A controlled post-sintering thermal or thermomechanical treatment can generate an ultrathin graded diffusion layer at the W–Cu interface.
The graded W–Cu interfacial layer will reduce interfacial thermal resistance.
Reducing interfacial thermal resistance will increase the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The treatment can increase thermal conductivity without degrading mechanical durability.
The treatment can increase thermal conductivity without degrading irradiation resistance.
Conventionally sintered W–Cu composites have sharp, poorly bonded W–Cu interfaces.
A sharp, poorly bonded W–Cu interface limits thermal transport.
Treatment temperature, duration, and cooling rate can be optimized to control formation of a nanometer-scale interfacial diffusion zone.
Fusion-reactor joints and related heat-dissipation components operate under high thermal loads and irradiation exposure.
Fusion-reactor joint and high-power heat-dissipation service includes elevated temperatures and thermal cycling.
A graded interfacial diffusion layer can bridge lattice mismatch between tungsten and copper.
A graded W–Cu interface minimizes phonon and electron scattering by reducing abrupt changes at the phase boundary.
Improved interfacial continuity enhances thermal transport.
A heat-treatment-induced graded interface can improve metallurgical bonding and mechanical properties.
Strong interfacial metallurgical bonding will preserve irradiation durability.
The treated composite will have higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable untreated W–Cu composite.
An excessively thick interfacial layer or brittle intermetallic phases could compromise mechanical integrity and irradiation resistance.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement depends on optimizing the treatment parameters within a processing window that avoids excessive diffusion.
